messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy-five-year-old Martín, a married QA Engineer with Latin American heritage, experienced a devastating natural disaster that continues to haunt him. The event—a wildfire that swept through his community during an unusually dry and hot summer—left indelible marks on both his physical surroundings and his mental landscape. Martín vividly remembers the intense heat and the acrid smell of smoke that filled the air. He had been at work, running quality assurance tests for a project deadline, when he received a call from his wife, Ana. She was panicked, describing the flames licking at their home’s perimeter. He immediately rushed to her side, but by then, it was too late; the inferno had consumed their beloved neighborhood. The visual of fire and flames engulfing everything they owned remains seared into his memory. Since that day, Martín has become hypersensitive to triggers reminiscent of that fateful event. Even a hint of smoke or similar weather conditions can send him spiraling back to those harrowing moments. These triggers have led him to adopt maladaptive strategies in an attempt to cope with the overwhelming memories and emotions. He often finds himself ruminating on what he could have done differently to prevent the disaster, blaming himself for not being able to save their home or belongings. This self-blame only amplifies his distress, creating a vicious cycle where his negative thoughts exacerbate his symptoms. Martín's hypervigilance is another prominent feature of his post-traumatic experience. He constantly monitors his environment for signs of fire or smoke, becoming easily startled by any sudden sounds or changes in the weather. This constant state of alertness has taken a significant toll on both his physical and mental well-being. His body reacts strongly to any reminders of that stressful experience, leading him to feel jumpy and anxious much of the time. His heightened sense of threat is further exacerbated by these triggers. Whenever he smells smoke or sees flames, Martín's heart races, and he feels an overwhelming urge to flee or protect himself and Ana from another such catastrophe. These physical reactions only reinforce his maladaptive strategies, pushing him deeper into a cycle of rumination and self-blame. Martín’s work as a QA Engineer has also been affected by these symptoms. He often finds it difficult to focus on his projects, frequently distracted by thoughts of how the event could have been prevented or what he should have done differently. His preoccupation with these ideas makes it challenging for him to engage fully in his job duties and can lead to mistakes that he then dwells upon. Despite his efforts to suppress these memories and avoid triggers, Martín finds himself constantly haunted by them. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and increased threat perception has become overwhelming. He had come to believe that every gust of wind or whiff of smoke could be the harbinger of another disaster, which in turn deepened his sense of vulnerability. What finally brought Martín to seek help was a recent incident where he smelled something burning while at work. His reaction was so severe that it left him unable to function for several days. He realized then that these symptoms were not only affecting his daily life but also causing significant distress and disruption in his relationship with Ana. Despite feeling ashamed of his reactions, Martín is most hopeful for a way to regain control over his thoughts and emotions, to find peace from the constant reminders of that tragic day. In his current state, Martín fears being forever trapped in this cycle of heightened threat perception and maladaptive coping strategies. He hopes to learn how to manage these symptoms effectively so he can return to leading a fulfilling life with Ana without the looming specter of that devastating wildfire.
